chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
title: Breaking every rule at Chicago's La Salle Hotel
summary: Despite signs banning drinking and sitting with customers, the band filled their lockers with bottles, sat at tables, played loud at dinner and packed the room for five months instead of four weeks.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: See, John Kirby is cooking in that place. So then we started to playing around, like Chicago, the La Salle Hotel, I told you they shot the tear gas gun in the back. It was a class hotel, you know, and the man's got all the signs up there, you know, and Stuff brings this chick in and we play "Stompin' at the Savoy" and he's playing (sings "I love you") to this chick, because - they had been drinking all day. And Mr. Smith wouldn't talk to him at all, the manager. So — He only talked to me, you know. Because the sign's up there as big as can be. "Musicians. No drinking. No sitting with the customers. No standing at the bar. No bottles brought into the hotel at all." Not into the lockers or no way. We had those lockers full within a week. We had all kinds of bottles in there. The first night we were standing at the bar and Stuff was sitting at a table, and the next night we were all sitting at the tables, you know. And so the thing about that was -- another thing about that was we had to play that hour for dinner, as I said, when we first went in there the man said, "Keep it down, soft, during dinner," and we didn't. We went in there and played loud, all the numbers we used to play, and long numbers, you know, and building all the time. And people got so they liked it. The place had been a graveyard. The waiters and everything said, "This place has been a graveyard before you all come in here." And we got people used to listening to that stuff, and we packed that place, you know.

They'd come in at dinner and everything, you know. So now Smith, the manager, said, "You can't play loud, Jonah, because it gives them indigestion. It's too loud." So we'd play soft, and people would say, "No, come on, play loud. Play loud." They wanted it, you know. We were supposed to be in there for four weeks. We stayed five months.
